articles.title: Get tested and talk to your partner: how to have safer sex after age 50
articles.summary: At 51, I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide. When I got divorced after 28 years of monogamy, I was excited to be having sex again, but had concerns.
body: Now, at 51, I’ve been wondering how important barrier protection is for me. Though I haven’t hit menopause, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) says that “by 45 getting pregnant naturally is unlikely”, and HIV/Aids prevention and treatment have improved significantly in the last three decades.
When I consulted with my physician, she said I should still “be careful” but didn’t provide specific guidelines.

Frustrated, I started researching. I found books on safer sex for older adults, such as Never Too Late: Your Guide to Safer Sex after 60 by Dr Shannon Dowler. But I wanted something more concise, like the pamphlets we saw as teens. I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide, with expert advice about how to have safer sex as an older adult.
No sex is totally risk-free – at any age. This reality is reflected in the American Medical Association (AMA) using the term “safer sex” since the mid-90s, rather than “safe sex”.

articles.title: A job that changed me: I cried nearly every day working in aged care, then realised I could bring joy instead
articles.summary: I once asked a resident what she would do if she could do anything. She replied: ‘I’d run in a field’ In my 40s, I was beginning to wonder where I fit in the employment world.
body: Living in Sydney, with my kids at school and a mortgage to pay, I took on some temp work through an agency.

I was placed in an aged care residential home, working on reception. Within the first hour I was in tears. I was really confronted by the residents as I hadn’t been around older people much before, especially people with dementia. I worked there for a month and cried every day.

A few months later the temp agency called again. The same aged care company had some full-time reception work at another residence, and had requested “the lady who cried all the time”. I took the job.

On my first day I was nervous. I didn’t want people’s first impressions of me to be someone who was too sensitive to work there. At one point I found myself in the bathroom letting go of a couple of tears and gave myself a good pep talk.

articles.title: The hill I will die on: Karaoke is not karaoke unless you sing with strangers | Kelli Blanchett
articles.summary: Community, camaraderie, socialism: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesis. On a gloomy Wednesday evening, my best friend and I decided we wanted to scratch our singing itch.
body: Private karaoke booths are sticky little cubicles for people who like singing but don’t want to be seen. They’re places where you pay a premium to avoid rubbing shoulders with strangers or making new connections. The whole point is to avoid exposure to the real world, which fundamentally misunderstands the power of karaoke.

I grew up in a former steel town. Twice a week, my mum hosted karaoke at a local pub, and because we couldn’t afford a babysitter, my sister and I went with her. When Mum’s caring responsibilities for my dad increased, she passed on the mantle to me, aged 17, to earn a bit of cash and keep the family business alive. Sitting with strangers across generations, hearing the stories behind their song choices, sharing rounds of drinks and political opinions, I felt like a sponge, soaking up different walks of life.

This is why when I talk about karaoke I’m not picturing these private, pay-by-the-hour cells. I’m thinking about the working-class pubs and clubs of Britain, where coming face to face with your community was more than half the point.
points: Community, camaraderie, socialism: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights.
On a gloomy Wednesday evening, my best friend and I decided we wanted to scratch our singing itch.

articles.title: Harry Styles walked eight miles in loafers. Is he ruining his feet? There’s only one way to find out
articles.summary: For his trek across New York City, the singer wore a pair of Prada slip-ons. I tried to do the same in my penny loafers – and soon found out why experts advise against it.
body: Last month, just before his 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, Harry Styles was spotted walking the streets of New York. According to the paparazzi who trailed him throughout his journey, he walked eight miles – all the way from Brooklyn into Manhattan – in loafers.

If, like me, you own a pair of loafers, your first thought is probably: that doesn’t sound like a good idea. On Instagram, Grazia called Styles’ shoes “perhaps the least sensible footwear for such an undertaking”.

You might imagine that single outing would have taught Styles a lesson, but he was photographed a few days later in the same pair of loafers, which all the evidence suggests are dark brown, pre-distressed Prada “Shuffle” shoes that cost £910. At that price I wouldn’t even wear them outside – they look soft and flimsy, like a cross between a moccasin and a ballet slipper.

However, following Styles’ example, I’m suddenly determined to get more mileage out of my own, underused slip-ons. I mean to wear them every day, all day, for a week – and to walk at least eight miles in them, if not in one day, then at least cumulatively.

articles.title: How to Throw a Garden Party Like the Meyers Family
articles.summary: Vogue’s Eileen Kelly pays a visit to Annie Meyers-Shyer’s idyllic book launch for ‘This Oak House,’ held in the back garden of her mom Nancy Meyers’s Los Angeles home.
body: It was an 80-degree Sunday in Los Angeles when I wound my way down the PCH toward Sunset and pulled up to a gate with a valet out front. Inside, a pea-gravel driveway flanked by manicured hedges led me to a white house with roses climbing perfectly across its facade. It looked exactly like a Nancy Meyers movie set—which, it turns out, was because I was actually at Nancy Meyers’s house.

We were there to celebrate the launch of This Oak House, Nancy’s daughter Annie Meyers-Shyer’s new book about renovating her 1940s Beverly Hills home, out now. After passing a table stacked with copies of the book, we made our way into the backyard, where the party looked exactly like the kind of party you would expect to happen at Meyers’s house: blonde and brunette balayaged women in Dôen dresses and Foundrae necklaces, many wearing enormous hats to shield themselves from the sun.

Waiters circulated with chip bags filled with black caviar, miniature lobster rolls, and Hugo spritzes. I was grateful I had convinced my boyfriend to come with me, because I didn’t know a single person and wasn’t prepared to make small talk while holding a tiny bag of caviar.
points: Vogue’s Eileen Kelly pays a visit to Annie Meyers-Shyer’s idyllic book launch for ‘This Oak House,’ held in the back garden of her mom Nancy Meyers’s Los Angeles home.

articles.title: At Casa Tua, the CFDA Brought Fashion’s Past, Present, and Future Together
articles.summary: The Council of Fashion Designers of America and Madison Avenue Business Improvement District (BID) hosted the third annual Step Up for Fashion. Set against the art-filled interiors of The Club at Casa Tua, the initiative championed emerging talent and raised support for the CFDA Scholarship Fund.
body: Designers, retail directors, and CFDA members were greeted with bubbly mimosas and ushered towards a spread of flaky croissants, fresh fruit, and much-needed coffee after a bustling fashion week. At the heart of the room, the work of four student scholarship recipients—Aneska Ryzada, Giang Luu, Chris Ortiz, and Kineri Shah—was prominently displayed.

“The present and the past have no meaning unless we look into the future,” CFDA board member Prabal Gurung told Vogue. “When I look at these new designers, I see hope about where the industry can go. I’m blown away by the level of talent.”

Basque-waist gowns, feathered tulle, corseted bodices, and intricate layering showcased impeccable design technique and creativity. Bethann Hardison, Tara Rudes Dann, and Lauren Kulchinsky Levison were amongst those who lingered over the work, taking in the intricate details. “As someone who just came to America, I feel so welcome and supported,” scholarship winner Anezka Rysada said while standing beside her garment reminiscent of Renaissance jester fashion.
points: The Council of Fashion Designers of America and Madison Avenue Business Improvement District (BID) hosted the third annual Step Up for Fashion.

articles.title: Taylor Swift Rocks a $40 Tank Top to Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game
articles.summary: Sporting some super affordable Chiefs merch—designed by a close friend—Taylor Swift made sure to let the Jumbotron know: “That’s my husband!”
body: Last night, the Kansas City Chiefs played off against the Indianapolis Colts at the Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri. And whenever tight-end Travis Kelce is playing on the field, you can count on wife Taylor Swift to be close by—to cheer him on in the stands, of course.

The pop star was joined by her parents, Scott and Andrea Swift, in their private suite to watch the game. (The Chiefs won!) And naturally, Swift wore her best red and white Chiefs merch for the occasion. The star wore a $40 tank top from the official Chiefs merch website, and the affordable piece was designed by the sports commentator and TV personality Erin Andrews, who happens to be a close friend of Swift’s. We love friends supporting friends.

The sweetest moment of last night’s game, though? That’s when Kelce scored his first touchdown of the match: Taylor Swift pointed to her wedding band and Kindred Lubeck engagement ring, proudly proclaiming on the Jumbotron, “That’s my husband!”

articles.title: Salut! Gap and A.P.C. Toasted to Their Collaboration in SoHo
articles.summary: On Thursday evening, an effortlessly cool crowd slipped past blue velvet ropes and filled the A.P.C. flagship store to celebrate the launch of the new collaboration.
body: Utility jackets, striped tees, and cable-knit cardigans hung from industrial pipe racks, bridging Parisian sophistication and American ease. The collection itself stemmed from an organic friendship between Gap Inc.’s creative director Zac Posen and A.P.C.’s Jean and Judith Touitou. Influences from the two distinct fashion capitals, spanning “both sides of the ocean,” were on the mood board, Judith Touitou told Vogue. “It’s a mutual journey that these brands have been on,” Posen added. “It’s about the great democratization of fashion and making great classics that never go out of style.”

Among the guests at the launch celebration were Coco Rocha and Debbie Harry, weaving through the space and stopping at the backlit bar for drinks, nodding along to the sounds of DJ duo Las Flaquitas. Attendees also paused to take in the short film, The Long Way, which was being projected onto the wall. Directed by Karl Cannone, styled by Alastair McKimm, and overseen by Gap’s creative director Calvin Leung, the rom-com-esque film transported guests to Paris’s Montmartre neighborhood as a cross-cultural story, starring American rapper ian and French DJ Paloma Le Friant, unfolded.

articles.title: Easy Spaghetti With Kale and Garlic
articles.summary: Lots of garlic, lots of Parm, and an entire crisper drawer’s worth of kale.
body: This spaghetti with kale is what happens when aglio e olio meets an entire crisper drawer’s worth of greens. The recipe calls for a seemingly absurd amount of kale, but don’t worry: A quick blanch in salted water—the same water you’ll use to cook the pasta—seasons and softens the greens. Several minutes in garlicky olive oil then transform them into silky ribbons that tangle easily with the pasta.

The sauce is simple but satisfying: olive oil, lots of garlic, black pepper, and starchy pasta water, tossed with the spaghetti until everything turns glossy. Parmesan and red pepper flakes finish the job, making this easy kale pasta savory, spicy, and deeply satisfying—the kind of 30-minutes-or-less dinner that earns a spot in the weeknight rotation.

Cook 3 large or 4 small bunches kale (any type; about 1½ lb.), stems and ribs removed, leaves torn crosswise into 2"–3" pieces, in a large pot of boiling salted water until bright green and slightly softened, about 2 minutes. Using tongs, transfer kale to a colander and rinse under cold running water, tossing; squeeze out excess liquid from leaves. Keep water in pot at a boil (you’ll use it for the pasta).
